title: Sweat Cools Only When It Evaporates

scenes.tts: A gram of sweat that evaporates from your skin carries off about two point four kilojoules of heat. A gram that drips off carries away almost none. So the cooling comes from evaporation, not from sweat itself. Sweat cools you only as fast as air takes up water vapour. On a humid day, that can lag behind the heat your muscles make.
scenes.visual: Two drops on skin blocks: one evaporates and carries heat away, one drips off; then a short bar for vapour uptake lags a long bar for muscle heat.

scenes.tts: For a person, heat balance is a sum. Heat storage equals metabolic rate, minus external work, plus or minus dry exchange, minus evaporative loss. Dry exchange means radiant, convective and conductive heat, and it can run either way. Every term is in watts. When storage is zero, body temperature is steady.
scenes.visual: The equation S = (M - W) +/- R +/- C +/- K - E builds up term by term in term colours with plain-word labels; then heat-in and heat-out bars appear and match, storage reads zero.

scenes.tts: Take illustrative numbers for a healthy seventy kilogram adult cycling steadily in hot, sunny air. Metabolic rate is one thousand watts, and twenty percent of it becomes external work. That leaves eight hundred watts of heat. Dry heat gain adds fifty watts, and respiratory heat loss is ignored. To keep storage at zero, evaporation must remove eight hundred fifty watts.
scenes.visual: A 1,000 W bar loses a 200 W work slice, leaving 800 W; a 50 W dry-gain slice is added; the heat-out bar grows to 850 W.

scenes.tts: Evaporating sweat takes up about two point four three kilojoules per gram at skin temperature. So eight hundred fifty watts needs about one point two six litres of sweat per hour, if every gram evaporates. Suppose only seventy percent evaporates and the rest drips. The sweat rate then rises to about one point eight litres per hour. Without drinking, body mass falls about two point six percent in that hour.
scenes.visual: A sweat bar of 1.26 L per h, all evaporated (blue); it grows by a grey dripped part to 1.80 L per h with the 70 percent / 30 percent split; a body-mass readout shows 2.6 percent.
scenes.caption: Evaporating sweat takes up about 2.43 kJ per g at skin temperature. So 850 W needs about 1.26 L of sweat per hour, if every gram evaporates. Suppose only 70 percent evaporates and the rest drips. The sweat rate then rises to about 1.80 L per hour. Without drinking, body mass falls about 2.6 percent in that hour.

scenes.tts: Now let humid air cap evaporation at seven hundred watts, when the body needs eight hundred fifty. The gap of one hundred fifty watts is stored as heat, five hundred forty kilojoules in an hour. Take two point nine eight kilojoules per kilogram per degree Celsius. Then seventy kilograms stores about two hundred nine kilojoules per degree. If body temperature is uniform, it rises about two point six degrees Celsius per hour.
scenes.visual: Required bar 850 W against a heat-out bar stopped at a yellow humid-air cap at 700 W; the 150 W gap fills red; a chain 540 kJ per h, 209 kJ per degree, 2.6 degrees C per h appears.
scenes.caption: Now let humid air cap evaporation at 700 W, when the body needs 850 W. The gap of 150 W is stored as heat, 540 kJ in an hour. Take 2.98 kJ per kg per degree C. Then 70 kg stores about 209 kJ per degree. If body temperature is uniform, it rises about 2.6 degrees C per hour.

scenes.tts: Once evaporation reaches the most that air allows, sweating harder adds dripping, not cooling. Balance returns three ways. Make less heat by slowing down. Take in less dry heat with shade or cooler air. Or have drier air. These numbers are made up for practice, and the rate predicts no real person. Keep this rule. Sweat cools only when it evaporates, and the air sets how much can.
scenes.visual: A sketch plot of evaporative cooling against sweat secreted rises then flattens at the cap under the required line; extra sweat drips; three levers move a line until required and cap meet.
